title: Rivian spinoff Also to start delivering e-bikes after months of delays
teaser: After massive delays blamed on supply chains, Rivian's spinoff Also is finally set to deliver its $4,500 e-bikes next week.
summary: Rivian's spinoff, Also, announced it will finally begin delivering its e-bikes next week, ending months of delays. The Launch Edition TM-B model retails for $4,500. Initially developed as a skunkworks project in 2022 and spun out into its own company in March 2025 with $105 million funding from Eclipse, the delivery was postponed due to global supply chain pressures affecting raw materials and components. While Also plans future vehicles for Amazon cargo transport and DoorDash autonomous delivery, the current focus is on deliveries amidst growing customer frustration over repeated delays and poor communication.
author: Sean O'Kane
content: Rivian spinoff Also will finally start delivering its first e-bikes to customers next week, after months of delays related to unspecified supply chain issues. The company told TechCrunch on Friday that the Launch Edition of its TM-B e-bike, which retails for $4,500, has started shipping from its manufacturer to its warehouse in the U.S. Also said it expects to deliver all Launch Edition bikes between next week and September. Also began as a skunkworks project inside Rivian in 2022, after CEO RJ Scaringe started looking into making an e-bike to complement his portfolio of electric vehicles for the outdoorsy set. The company spent a few years tinkering with the idea, and even hired Jony Ive's design firm LoveFrom to help with an early design, as TechCrunch first reported in 2025. In March 2025, Rivian spun out Also as its own company, with $105 million in backing from Eclipse. The startup revealed its first e-bike, the TM-B, in October of last year. It originally targeted a "spring" 2026 ship date, but supply chain headaches got in the way, and the company pushed the delivery window to July. "The primary factor driving our updated summer timeline is current stress on global supply chains. A rapid, industry-wide spike in demand for raw materials and electronic components has impacted key parts required for the TM-B. This has temporarily delayed our planned manufacturing ramp-up and pushed our first delivery dates past our original spring window," the company wrote in June on a support page . "Our engineering and production teams are working around the clock to minimize these constraints without cutting a single corner on safety or quality." Also declined to say what components, specifically, caused the delay. Also has big plans beyond the TM-B. The startup mostly refers to itself as a "vehicle" company and has plans to make four-wheel pedal-assist cargo vehicles for Amazon. The company is working on an autonomous delivery vehicle for DoorDash, too. But for now, Also needs to focus on delivering its first e-bikes while navigating the next set of headaches for a company shipping products like these: customer service. On Friday, the last day of July, a number of customers were venting in a thread in the r/ALSOmicromobility subreddit about the repeated delays. "I'm really frustrated by the lack of communication and the actual miscommunication/lies from Also regarding shipment timelines," the original poster wrote . "Why do they keep making these promises about shipping timelines just to blow right past them without any communication or actual updates? It really makes no sense." "Hey we've still got a few business hours left in July. Maybe we'll get an email later this morning ☺️," a different user responded. Not everyone was so patient. "Couldn't wait any longer and canceled my reservation," another wrote.

title: With Switch 2, iPhone, and laptop tricks, the Sharge Disk Pro 2 is finally a worthy EDC
teaser: The Sharge Disk Pro 2 Ultra is touted as an all-in-one USB-C Swiss Army Knife, docking everything from MacBooks to iPhone and even Switch 2.
summary:
Sharge has released the Disk Pro 2 Ultra, a portable SSD enclosure that functions as a powerful USB-C hub and external dock. It provides a single solution for multiple gadgets, including laptops, tablets, phones, and Nintendo Switch/Switch 2. Key features include a 4K 144Hz HDMI 2.1 output, storage support for up to 8TB via M.2 SSDs, and connectivity options like SD/microSD readers and USB-C PD charging.

The review highlights its immense versatility, allowing connection of multiple peripherals (monitor, keyboard, etc.) with one cord. However, the article cautions users about power limitations: while convenient for portability, operating heavy loads (like 4K ProRes video recording or large data transfers) requires plugging in an external USB-C battery.

Compatibility notes include the need for high wattage (85W+) charging for Switch 2 and the acknowledgment that some advanced features, like Variable Refresh Rate (VRR), may not function correctly through the dock. Despite minor flaws reported during testing, it is considered a significant upgrade over previous Sharge models due to improved design and built-in magnetic attachment.
author: Sean Hollister
content: Sharge, the company that makes delightful retro Mac-shaped chargers and see-inside batteries , is finally impressing me with a portable SSD. I couldn't recommend the Sharge Disk, Disk Plus, or even the Disk Pro, but I'd be happy to own the new Disk Pro 2 Ultra . This isn't just a drive. It's a 4K HDMI dock and a USB-C hub too. It's a veritable USB-C Swiss Army Knife for all your main gadgets: laptop, tablet, phone, Steam Deck, even the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2. And this USB multitool has built-in MagSafe pattern magnets to stick it to your iPhone, Pixel, or anything where you're willing to stick a magnetic ring. (One stick-on ring is included.) In total, this pack-of-playing-cards-sized gadget adds one 4K 144Hz HDMI 2.1 video output, a 5Gbps USB-A port, SD and microSD card readers, plus USB-C passthrough charging - plus a slot to add up to 8TB of solid-state storage with a full-sized M.2 2280 (or smaller M.2 2242 and 2230) stick SSDs. By plugging in a single cord, I gave my MacBook Pro a second external monitor, four simultaneous sources of storage (SSD, USB flash drive, SD, microSD), and 80W of USB-C PD juice. And when I plugged in my Android phone and a USB-C iPhone, both of them saw the SSD and showed up on my HDMI screen. It also unlocked 4K60 ProRes video recording on the iPhone... more on that in a minute. Some of these features exist together in other gadgets , and this 10Gbps external SSD enclosure certainly isn't the fastest in town now that 40Gbps and 80Gbps enclosures exist. With big 100GB and 195GB transfers, my write speeds with a budget 1TB Lexar NM710 in the Disk Pro 2 averaged around 700MB/s. I stuck a magnetic ring to my MacBook so I could hang the Disk Pro 2 on the back of its lid. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge But that's still nothing to sneeze at, and how many enclosures double as USB-C HDMI docks, let alone ones that speak Nintendo's language and magnetically attach to your phone? How many have a built-in fan to keep them cool? And how many are low-power enough that you can power the HDMI and USB ports from your phone or laptop, no need for a power cord? Things get a little tricky with the low wattage, though. First, Sharge is selling two models of the Disk Pro 2, the "Ultra" that requires at least 1.5W of USB-C bus power, and and the "Lite" which needs 5W for its more power-hungry chips (and only does 4K60 over HDMI 2.0, instead of 4K144 over HDMI 2.1). Second, to achieve such low power draw on the Ultra, it can only route 3W of power from your laptop or phone to a connected SSD, Sharge marketing manager Leo H. tells me. Reviews show my borrowed Lexar NM710 draws more than that during writes - and sure enough, the Disk Pro 2 shut down right after I started ProRes video recording on an iPhone 15 Pro or a big transfer on my Galaxy S25. (There's a simple solution: just plug an external USB-C battery or charger into the Disk Pro 2. When I did that, I recorded over five minutes of 4K60 ProRes video, no problem. You could instead try to find a lower-power SSD.) The main HDMI, USB-A, and USB-C charger port are all on one edge. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge Third, while the HDMI dock does work with both my Switch 2 and my original Switch, Nintendo's handhelds explicitly check for a relatively specific external power source before docking. Sharge is still tweaking the firmware, but says I currently need a 85W or higher USB-C PD charger plugged in for Switch 2 in particular. You should also know there's a long pause before the Nintendo Switch and Switch 2 appear on a connected TV, like some other third-party docks, and you won't get variable refresh rate (VRR) with a Steam Deck or other PC handhelds. It does 4K144 and 4K120 with HDR, but the Steam Deck claims my VRR TV is not VRR-capable with the Disk Pro 2 as a go-between. And while I successfully worked with a mouse, keyboard, headset, monitor, webcam, and more plugged into the Disk Pro 2 for several days - by daisy-chaining an extra USB hub - I did occasionally see the monitor go dark for a minute, roughly once a day. There's still work for Sharge to do. But it's the first drive from the company that I'd happily add to my go bag. Sharge Disk (yellow), Disk Plus (silver), Disk Pro (fixed cable), and Disk Pro 2 (detachable cable). Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge The original Sharge Disk was a bulky dongle with a ridiculously noisy tiny fan. The Disk Plus marketed itself as barely-there stylishly thin SSD enclosure that magnetically attaches to your phone, but the magnets were actually a stick-on accessory that made the drive much thicker. The first Sharge Disk Pro had a power port so tiny and recessed that most charging cables wouldn't fit, and buttons that could actually cut power to the drive mid-transfer. IMO, Sharge should've done more user testing before releasing these predecessors. Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge The Disk Pro 2 fixes all that. The included cable is now detachable, the magnets are built-in, the ports are no longer weirdly recessed, the fan isn't noisy by default, you can turn off that fan entirely, the switch doesn't cut power to the drive, and the drive has a larger airflow path. Plus, you can bring your own SSD - though I'd prefer toolless swaps to the current screws. No more heavily recessed USB ports . Photo by Sean Hollister / The Verge You won't always see much higher transfer speeds turning that fan on full blast. My 195GB transfer took 4 minutes and 55 seconds with the fan on full power, and 5 minutes 5 seconds with it off - a difference of just 10 seconds, even though I let it cool between tests. The real difference is the one I felt when trying to pick up the Disk Pro 2 afterwards. Without fan, the metal sides were burning hot to the touch. The Disk Pro 2 Ultra is $75 on Kickstarter for early bird and will be $89 full retail. While the typical caveats apply with Kickstarter projects, Sharge has a very solid track record for shipping (even if it's hit and miss on design). title: Airport sign fails to boot, officers already on the scene
teaser: An airport digital sign failed spectacularly, booting up with a cryptic 'EFI Shell' error visible to passersby.
summary:
A digital signage unit at a Phoenix airport car rental building experienced a technical malfunction, failing to boot and displaying an 'EFI Shell' style prompt. This issue indicates potential underlying system problems, such as missing required drive or filesystem mappings. Although police officers were spotted on site, the article suggests the glitch is merely a minor IT failure that needs technical repair rather than intervention by authorities.

The EFI Shell prompt usually appears when a computer cannot boot normally and requires manual loading of drivers or boot loaders by an experienced user.
content: OFFBEAT Airport sign fails to boot, officers already on the scene Bork! Bork! That's the sound of the police BORK!BORK!BORK! The sight of the police can make even the clearest conscience twitch. Perhaps the authorities have finally come to ask about that music track you copied 30 years ago. We're not saying the presence of the law sent this digital signage into a tizz, but you never know. Spotted by an eagle-eyed Register reader at a Phoenix airport car rental building, today's borked signage looks like the result of a PC in the background choking when trying to find a boot device. The EFI Shell looks much like a terminal prompt and usually appears because the system has failed to boot normally. An experienced user can use it to load drivers or boot loaders manually, but for the vast majority, it doesn't rear its head unless something is amiss. The system appears to have dropped into the EFI Shell instead of starting the signage software. Perhaps the expected drive or filesystem mapping has disappeared, or a startup script is looking for something that is no longer there. An experienced techie might be able to fix it, but the audience here is more likely to consist of harried passengers wondering whether EFI Shell is a new budget airline. And then there is the presence of the police. We know that some users find the approach to quality adopted by certain software vendors bordering on the criminal, but calling the cops on some borked signage seems a bit excessive. There doesn't appear to be anyone inside the vehicle, so perhaps the officers have gone in search of the IT operative responsible for the shoddy work that has left the digital sign in such a distressed state. Hopefully it won't give users ideas about how to escalate the ticket that IT appears to be studiously ignoring. Tech support, after all, is not the fourth emergency service, despite what that user with a dodgy mouse might think. ®

title: What makes a toy go viral
teaser: Discover the economics of viral toys: How do companies manufacture a 'hit' toy like squishy dumplings, moving beyond mere trends?
summary: This Planet Money podcast episode explores the economics behind why some toys, like 'squishy dumplings,' go viral. The discussion reveals that the trend is not just about anxiety relief or social media hype; it offers valuable insights into the entire process—from creation to manufacturing a successful product without financial risk. Listeners learn how to understand the economic forces that make play items profitable and sustainable.
content: Squishy, slimy, fidgety toys are having a moment. But it's more than just an anxiety-soothing, social-media fueled trend - these toys are reshaping how toys get made. Today on the show, we have the story of the once-humble squishy dumpling and what it teaches us about how to make a viral hit and how to manufacture it, without getting left holding the bag. Hear it all firsthand from the creator of this trendy toy.
